passages.t: A plot, a jar of perfume, and thirty pieces of silver
passages.happening:
Jesus finishes his teaching and tells his disciples plainly what is coming: “You know that the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (verse 2).

At the same time the chief priests and elders meet in the courtyard of the high priest, Caiaphas. They plan to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him, but not during the feast, in case the people riot.

In the village of Bethany, at the home of Simon the Leper, a woman pours a jar of very costly perfume on Jesus' head as he reclines at the table. The disciples are angry. “Why this waste?” they ask. It could have been sold and the money given to the poor. Jesus defends her. She has done a beautiful thing. She has prepared his body for burial, and wherever the gospel is preached, her story will be told.

Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests. “What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?” (verse 15). They count out thirty pieces of silver. From then on he looks for a chance to betray Jesus.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this part of the story too (Mark 14:1-11), and the note on Mark 14 explains the Passover crowds, the danger of a riot, the alabaster jar, the perfume and the meaning of anointing a head. Here are the things Matthew does differently.

In Matthew, Jesus speaks first. Before the leaders make their plan, he has already said that he will be handed over at the Passover. Nothing that follows takes him by surprise.

Matthew names the high priest: Caiaphas. Josephus says the Roman governor Valerius Gratus appointed a man called Joseph Caiaphas high priest around AD 18, and that he was removed by the Roman official Vitellius around AD 36 or 37 (Antiquities 18.35, 18.95). He held the post for many years, almost exactly while Pilate governed. That suggests he knew how to work with Rome. The note on Mark 14 tells of the burial box inscribed ‘Joseph son of Caiaphas’ found in 1990.

In Mark, ‘some’ at the table complain. In Matthew it is the disciples.

And in Matthew, Judas asks for money before he is promised it. Only Matthew names the sum: thirty pieces of silver. The coins were most likely silver shekels, perhaps the heavy silver coins of Tyre that were used to pay the temple tax, though the Gospel does not say which coin it means. The amount was not huge. Matthew's readers would have heard something else in it, from their Scriptures.
passages.ot:
In the law of Moses, thirty shekels of silver was the price paid to a master if an ox killed his slave: “the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to the master of that servant” (Exodus 21:32). It was what a slave's life was reckoned to be worth.

In Zechariah, a shepherd of God's people asks for his wages, and the people insult him with a slave's price: “So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver” (Zechariah 11:12). God tells him to throw it to the potter, calling it “this magnificent price at which they valued me” (Zechariah 11:13). The words are bitter. That is what they thought the shepherd was worth. Matthew uses the very same phrase, thirty pieces of silver, and he will come back to this passage when Judas returns the money (27:9-10).

Jesus' words about the poor echo Deuteronomy 15:11, which commands generosity; the note on Mark 14 explains them.
passages.hard:
Why did Judas do it? Matthew is the only Gospel where Judas asks for money first, so many readers think Matthew wants us to see greed. John says Judas stole from the common purse (John 12:6). But thirty pieces of silver was a modest sum, and many have wondered whether something more lay underneath: disappointment that Jesus was not the kind of Messiah he wanted, or a plan to force his hand. The Gospels do not say. Matthew sets the woman and Judas side by side, as Mark does. She pours out something precious on Jesus. He sells Jesus for the price of a slave.

It is worth saying plainly that Judas's story is not a story about Jews. His name is the Greek form of Judah, a common Jewish name. From the Middle Ages on, Judas was sometimes treated as a picture of the whole Jewish people, and that picture fed contempt for Jews. It is false. Judas was one Jew among twelve Jewish disciples. The others were Jews too, and so was the woman who anointed Jesus, and so was Jesus himself.
passages.asks: The disciples complained in the name of the poor. Jesus praised the woman in the name of love. Ask whether you ever use a good cause as a way of judging someone else's gift to God. And look at the price. Jesus was sold for what the law put on the life of a slave. Ask what you value him at.

passages.happening:
On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread the disciples ask Jesus where to prepare the Passover. He sends them into the city to a certain man with a message: “The Teacher says, ‘My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house’” (verse 18). They prepare the meal.

That evening, as they recline at the table, Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me” (verse 21). They are deeply grieved, and one by one they ask, “Surely not I, Lord?” (verse 22). Jesus says it is the one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with him. The Son of Man goes as it is written, but woe to the one who betrays him. It would have been better for him not to have been born.

Then Judas asks too: “Surely not I, Rabbi?” Jesus answers, “You have said it yourself” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 14:12-21), and the note on Mark 14 explains the Passover lambs, the rooms in the city, and the shame of betraying someone you have shared bread with.

Matthew adds two things. Jesus' message to the host says, ‘My time is near.’ Jesus knows his hour has come and he goes toward it freely.

And Matthew alone keeps the exchange with Judas. The other disciples call Jesus ‘Lord’. Judas calls him ‘Rabbi’, which means teacher. It was a respectful title, and a fair one, but in Matthew's story it stands out. Judas will use it again in the garden (verse 49).

‘You have said it yourself’ is an unusual answer. Jesus gives the same answer to the high priest (verse 64). Many scholars take it as a yes, but a careful one: it puts the words back on the person who asked. Judas has named himself.
passages.ot:
The bread shared from one bowl recalls a psalm of David about a friend who turned against him: “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9).

‘The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him’ points to the Scriptures as a whole. The Passover itself goes back to Exodus 12, where God told Israel to keep the feast every year in memory of how he brought them out of Egypt.
passages.hard:
If the Scriptures said the Son of Man would go this way, was Judas still to blame? Matthew holds both in one sentence: the Son of Man goes as it is written, “but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed” (verse 24). God's purpose stands, and Judas is responsible for what he chose. Joseph once said to the brothers who sold him, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). Christians from different traditions explain that tension in different ways, but none of them says Judas was a puppet.

‘It would be better for him if he had not been born’ is one of the hardest things Jesus says. It is a cry of grief and warning over a terrible choice. It does not tell us everything about Judas's end, and the next chapter will show his remorse (27:3). These notes do not claim to know what God finally did with him.

On the date of this meal, Matthew agrees with Mark that it was the Passover meal, while John seems to place it a day earlier. The note on Mark 14 sets out the answers Christians have given. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover time, on a Friday.
passages.asks: Every disciple at that table thought, at least for a moment, that it might be him. That is a healthy fear. Ask yourself the same question when you read of Judas and Peter: not ‘how could they?’ but ‘could I?’ Jesus still shared the bowl with the man who would betray him. He did not throw him out.

passages.t: This is My body; this is My blood, for the forgiveness of sins
passages.happening:
While they are eating, Jesus takes bread, speaks a blessing, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples: “Take and eat; this is My body” (verse 26). Then he takes a cup, gives thanks, and gives it to them. “Drink from it, all of you. This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (verses 27-28).

He tells them he will not drink of the fruit of the vine again until the day he drinks it new with them in his Father's kingdom. They sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 14:22-26), and the note on Mark 14 explains the Passover meal, the host who explained the food, and the hymn, most likely from Psalms 113 to 118.

Matthew's words differ in small ways that matter. ‘Take and eat.’ ‘Drink from it, all of you.’ And above all, only Matthew has the words ‘for the forgiveness of sins’. In Mark the blood is “poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). In Luke it is “poured out for you” (Luke 22:20). In Matthew Jesus says what it is for.

That phrase matters for the rest of Matthew's story. At the start of the book the angel said the child would be called Jesus “because He will save His people from their sins” (1:21). Here, on his last night, Jesus says how. And in the next chapter a crowd will cry out about his blood (27:25). Matthew has already told his readers what that blood is for.

Matthew alone also says ‘with you’: Jesus will drink it new ‘with you’ in his Father's kingdom. The promise is a meal together.
passages.ot:
At Mount Sinai Moses sealed God's covenant with blood and said, “This is the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). A covenant is a binding promise between God and his people. Jesus uses the same words for his own blood.

Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant ends with forgiveness: “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). Matthew's ‘for the forgiveness of sins’ points straight to that promise.

Isaiah's servant “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12), and Jesus had said that he came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (20:28).
passages.hard: What does ‘This is My body’ mean? Christians have read these words in different ways, and the disagreement is old and serious. The Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with, and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed churches teach that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and that believers feed on him by faith. Many Baptist and other churches see the meal mainly as a memorial, a way of remembering his death as he commanded (1 Corinthians 11:24). These notes do not settle the question. Every one of these churches agrees that Jesus gave this meal to his followers, that it points to his death for them, and that it looks ahead to the kingdom.
passages.asks: Jesus gave his friends a meal on the night one of them betrayed him and the rest deserted him. He told them his blood was poured out for the forgiveness of sins, and he told it to people who would need that forgiveness within hours. Ask whether you think you have to be good enough to come to his table. And notice his last promise that night: a meal ‘with you’ in his Father's kingdom.

passages.happening:
On the way, Jesus tells them, “This very night you will all fall away on account of Me” (verse 31). Scripture says, ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after he has risen, he will go ahead of them into Galilee.

Peter says that even if everyone else falls away, he never will. Jesus tells him that this very night, before the rooster crows, Peter will deny him three times. Peter answers, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You” (verse 35). All the other disciples say the same.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 14:27-31), and the note on Mark 14 explains it. To ‘fall away’ is to stumble and stop following. In that culture, a disciple's loyalty to his teacher was a matter of honour, and abandoning him in danger was shameful.

Matthew adds ‘this very night’ and ‘on account of Me’. The test will come soon, and it will come because of Jesus. Matthew has only one crowing of the rooster where Mark has two.

Notice what Jesus puts inside the bad news. Before Peter has even made his boast, Jesus has already promised to meet them again in Galilee. Matthew's Gospel will end on a mountain in Galilee with exactly that meeting (28:16).
passages.ot: The words come from the prophet Zechariah: “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7). In Zechariah it is the LORD who calls the sword against his shepherd. Jesus reads his death as part of God's purpose, and the scattering of the disciples as foretold.
passages.hard: Was Peter lying when he said he would die for Jesus? Almost certainly not. He meant it. That is the hard truth of the passage: a person can mean a promise with all their heart and still break it a few hours later. Sincerity is not the same as strength.
passages.asks: Peter trusted his own loyalty. Jesus did not. But Jesus also did not give up on Peter. Ask where you are most sure of yourself, and whether that confidence rests on you or on him. And notice that the promise of Galilee was spoken before the failure. Grace was waiting before Peter needed it.

passages.happening:
Jesus comes with his disciples to a place called Gethsemane. He takes Peter and the two sons of Zebedee further in and begins to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with Me” (verse 38).

He goes a little farther, falls face down, and prays, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will” (verse 39). He comes back and finds them sleeping. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” he asks Peter. “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak” (verses 40-41).

He goes away a second time and prays, “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done” (verse 42). Again he finds them asleep. He prays a third time, saying the same thing. Then he wakes them. The hour has come. His betrayer is near.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 14:32-42), and the note on Mark 14 explains the place, usually taken to mean ‘oil press’, and the cup as a picture of suffering and judgment.

Matthew lets us hear the second prayer in words. “May Your will be done” is the very line Jesus taught his disciples in the Lord's Prayer: “Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10). In the garden he prays his own prayer, and it costs him everything. The same prayer also asks not to be led into temptation (6:13), and here Jesus tells his friends to watch and pray so that they will not enter into temptation.

Where Mark keeps the Aramaic ‘Abba’, Matthew writes ‘My Father’. Matthew also adds that Jesus wanted them to watch ‘with Me’. He did not want to be alone.
passages.ot:
Jesus' words of sorrow echo a lament in the Psalms: “Why are you downcast, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5). The psalm-writer pours out his grief to God and still calls him “my God” (Psalm 42:11). Jesus does the same.

A ‘cup’ in the prophets could stand for the suffering God's judgment brings. Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem drinking “the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17).
passages.hard:
Why would the Son of God dread death and ask to be spared? Critics of Christianity have asked this since the early centuries. A god, they said, would not tremble. The church's answer has been that Jesus was truly human, with a real human soul and a real human will. He felt horror at death and at the cup, as a real man would. And he freely gave his will to the Father's. The scene shows not that he was less than God, but that he truly became one of us.

This passage also speaks to anyone who has known sorrow so heavy it felt like dying. Jesus did not hide that sorrow. He said it out loud, to his friends and to his Father. If you are in a place like that, you are not wrong to say so, and you should not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live.
passages.asks: Jesus' prayer has two halves, and both are honest. ‘Let this cup pass from Me’ is a real request. ‘Yet not as I will, but as You will’ is a real surrender. Ask whether you allow yourself to pray the first half, and whether you can pray the second. Notice also how gently Jesus speaks to his sleeping friends. He names their weakness, and he does not stop loving them.

passages.happening:
While Jesus is still speaking, Judas arrives with a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders. He has given them a signal: the one he kisses is the man. He goes straight to Jesus, says, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kisses him. Jesus calls him ‘friend’ and tells him to do what he came for (verse 50). They seize him.

One of Jesus' companions draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. “Put your sword back in its place,” Jesus says. “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword” (verse 52). He could ask his Father, and at once he would have more than twelve legions of angels. But then how would the Scriptures be fulfilled?

Jesus asks the crowd why they have come with weapons, as if he were an outlaw, when he sat teaching in the temple courts every day. All this has happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled. Then all the disciples desert him and run.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 14:43-52), and the note on Mark 14 explains it. A student often greeted his teacher with a kiss. That is what made Judas's signal work. In the dark, among the olive trees, it looked like respect.

‘Friend’ is a polite word with an edge. Matthew uses it only three times, each time to someone in the wrong: to the grumbling worker (20:13), to the guest without wedding clothes (22:12), and here to Judas.

A legion was a Roman army unit of about five thousand soldiers. Twelve legions would be a vast army. Jesus is not short of power. He chooses not to use it.

Only Matthew has the saying about the sword. John's Gospel tells us that the one who struck was Simon Peter and that the servant's name was Malchus (John 18:10). Luke adds that Jesus healed the servant's ear (Luke 22:51).
passages.ot:
Jesus says the Scriptures must be fulfilled. He has already pointed to Zechariah's shepherd struck and sheep scattered (verse 31, from Zechariah 13:7). Here it comes true as the disciples flee.

The betrayal with a kiss recalls the psalm about a friend “the one who shared my bread” (Psalm 41:9), and Jesus' refusal to strike back fits the servant in Isaiah who “offered My back to those who struck Me” (Isaiah 50:6).
passages.hard:
Does ‘all who draw the sword will die by the sword’ mean that a Christian may never use force? Christians have read it in more than one way. Some, in the peace churches, read it with the Sermon on the Mount (5:39) as a call to refuse violence altogether. Others read it as a word about this moment, and about the church's mission, which must never be carried forward by the sword, while they hold that governments may rightly use force to protect the innocent (Romans 13:4). These notes do not settle that question. All agree on what Jesus did that night: he refused to be defended by violence, and he healed rather than harmed.

Notice that ‘all the disciples deserted Him and fled’. Mark's note says it well: the first followers told the story of their own failure. The church has been honest about its failures from the start.
passages.asks: Jesus calls Judas ‘friend’ even as he is betrayed. He will not let Peter defend him with a sword. Ask whether, when you are wronged, your first move is the sword or the trust Jesus shows here. And ask where you are tempted to defend Jesus, or your church, or your side, by means he refused.

passages.happening:
They take Jesus to the house of Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders have gathered. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard and sits with the guards to see what will happen.

The chief priests and the whole council look for false testimony to put Jesus to death. Many false witnesses come forward, but nothing holds. At last two say he claimed, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’ Jesus is silent.

Then the high priest says, “I charge You under oath by the living God: Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God” (verse 63). “You have said it yourself,” Jesus answers. “But I say to all of you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven” (verse 64). The high priest tears his clothes and cries blasphemy. ‘He deserves to die,’ they answer. They spit in his face and strike him. Some slap him and mock, “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit You?” (verse 68).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 14:53-65), and the note on Mark 14 explains the council, called the Sanhedrin, the tearing of clothes, and what blasphemy means.

Matthew sharpens a few things. In Matthew the council is looking for false testimony from the start. And in the end two witnesses agree. The law needed two or three witnesses to settle a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), so Matthew shows the council at last getting two witnesses to agree.

The high priest's words, ‘I charge You under oath by the living God’, were a formal demand. A person charged like that was bound to answer. The law of Moses made it a sin to stay silent when you heard such a public charge (Leviticus 5:1). That may be why Jesus, silent until now, speaks.

Jesus answers ‘You have said it yourself’, the same answer he gave Judas (verse 25). Where Mark has Jesus say plainly ‘I am’, Matthew keeps this careful yes and adds ‘from now on’. From this night, the one on trial will be seen as the judge.

The mocking is crueller in Matthew: “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit You?” They mock him as a prophet at the very moment his prophecy about Peter is coming true outside.
passages.ot:
Jesus' answer joins two Old Testament passages. Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, “Sit at My right hand.” And Daniel 7:13, where “One like the Son of Man” comes “with the clouds of heaven” to receive a kingdom from God. He is claiming to share God's throne.

His silence before false witnesses recalls Isaiah's servant: “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). And the spitting and slapping recall the servant who “did not hide My face from scorn and spittle” (Isaiah 50:6).
passages.hard:
Was this a lawful trial? The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, gives rules for a court in a capital case. The trial must be held by day. A guilty verdict must wait until the next day, so such a case is not heard on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1). By those rules, a night hearing at Passover breaks the law.

But scholars disagree on what that shows. Some think the Mishnah's rules, or something like them, were already in force, so the hearing was unlawful. Others point out that the Mishnah was written down long after the temple fell, and that it may describe the ideal law of later teachers rather than how the high priest's council actually worked in the 30s. On that view, it cannot be used to judge this hearing with certainty. Matthew himself does not argue the legal point. He simply shows that the plan to kill Jesus was made before the hearing began (26:4), and that the council went looking for false witnesses.

It matters to read this scene carefully. Matthew names particular people: Caiaphas, and the chief priests, elders, and scribes of that council. He does not blame the Jewish people, and Jesus, his disciples, and the crowds who loved him were all Jews. The note on 27:25 says more about how this story has been misused.
passages.asks: Jesus stays silent when lied about, and speaks plainly when put under oath. He does not defend himself, but he does not deny the truth to save his life. Ask whether you are more likely to defend your reputation or to tell the truth about Jesus when it costs you. Peter, at that same moment, was choosing the first.

passages.happening: Peter is sitting out in the courtyard. A servant girl comes up and says, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean” (verse 69). He denies it in front of them all: “I do not know what you are talking about.” He goes out to the gateway, and another servant girl tells the people there, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth” (verse 71). He denies it again, this time with an oath: “I do not know the man!” A little later those standing nearby say, “Surely you are one of them,” and, “your accent gives you away” (verse 73). Peter begins to curse and swear, “I do not know the man!” At once a rooster crows. Peter remembers what Jesus said, and he goes outside and weeps bitterly.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 14:66-72), and the note on Mark 14 explains it. A servant girl had little standing in that world. Peter, who had promised to face death, is undone by the question of a girl with no power over him at all.

Only Matthew says that Peter's accent gave him away. People from Galilee spoke with an accent people in Jerusalem could hear. Much later, the Babylonian Talmud keeps stories that poke fun at Galileans for not pronouncing some sounds clearly (Eruvin 53b).

Matthew makes the denials grow. First Peter denies it ‘before them all’. Then he denies it with an oath. Then he curses and swears. Notice the contrast with the scene inside. Jesus, under oath before the high priest, tells the truth and is condemned. Peter, under oath before servants, lies and goes free. And Jesus had taught, “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (5:37).

Matthew tells this story in full, with no attempt to make Peter look better. The early church told it about its own leader.
passages.ot:
The scene fulfils Jesus' own words in verse 34 and the scattering of Zechariah 13:7, which Jesus quoted on the way to the garden.

Peter's tears belong with the laments of Scripture, where sorrow for sin is brought before God and not hidden. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).
passages.hard:
Matthew mentions one crowing of the rooster, where Mark has two. Some manuscripts of Mark also have only one, which shows that copyists noticed the difference. It does not change the story: Peter denied Jesus three times that night, just as Jesus said.

The harder question is whether Peter's failure was the end of him. Matthew answers it later. After the resurrection the angel and Jesus send word to ‘His disciples’ and ‘My brothers’ (28:7, 28:10), and Peter is among the eleven who meet Jesus on the mountain in Galilee (28:16). John tells how Jesus restored him (John 21:15-19). He had not been dropped.

Matthew places Peter's bitter tears right before Judas's remorse (27:3-5). Both men failed Jesus on the same night. The note on 27:3-10 speaks about Judas with care.
passages.asks: Peter wept. Ask whether there is a failure you have stopped believing God could forgive. The rooster was a sound of shame for Peter. It also proved that Jesus had known all along and had chosen him anyway. If shame over something you have done feels too heavy to carry, you do not have to carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone you trust.
